raw_case_text:
A 59-year-old man was admitted to our hospital for the treatment of centrally located squamous cell-lung carcinoma and pulmonary tuberculosis. The computed tomography (CT) scans showed that the malignant lesion, located between the left upper and lower lobes, had invaded the left pulmonary artery ( Figure 1 ). Pathological and etiological findings revealed a combined diagnosis of squamous cell-lung cancer (T3N0M0) and pulmonary tuberculosis. Anti-tuberculosis therapy, which including Isoniazid (300 mg per day), Rifampicin (450 mg per day), Ethambutol (750 mg per day), and Pyrazinamide (1250 mg per day), without any adverse events, was administered to cure the pulmonary tuberculosis. Neoadjuvant therapy, including sintilimab and conventional chemotherapy, was administered to achieve a complete response (CR) or partial response (PR). After three cycles of neoadjuvant therapy, the patient underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) left lower lobectomy, because the malignant lesion had shrunk and the left pulmonary artery had been isolated from the tumor. No cutaneous toxicity was observed during the first three cycles of neoadjuvant therapy. According to the post-operative pathologic results, the neoadjuvant therapy resulted in a PR. Therefore, the sintilimab and conventional therapy were continued as post-operative adjuvant therapy.
Ten days after the post-operative adjuvant therapy, the patient suffered severe TEN, which rapidly progressed to cover >50% of the skin. TEN was associated with rashes of the trunk, pruritus, and a fever of >40 C. Massive maculopapular were observed in the chest and abdomen. Oral mucositis was also observed. The cutaneous lesions accounted for approximately 95% of the whole body surface ( Figure 2 ). No pulmonary, gastrointestinal, or cardiac AEs were presented in this patient. Physical examinations showed the positive Nikolsky sign. Laboratory results showed that the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), C-reactive protein was 3.48, 217.39 and 53.28, respectively. The white blood cell was lower than normal because of chemotherapy. Due to financial constraints, no further skin biopsies were taken for pathological analysis. Because of the shortage of pathologic results, a dermatologist diagnosed TEN due to the history of sintilimab use, epidermal necrolysis, positive Nikolsky sign, high NLR and PLR, and so on. Exfoliative dermatitis, which was similar to TEN was suspected, but the Nikolsky sign was negative. Intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg per day) was administered to this patient immediately. Additionally, prednisone (60 mg per day) was prescribed for out-patient use. Supportive management included wound care, nutritional supplementation, and analgesic use. Furthermore, Levofloxacin (500 mg per day) was administered to treat infections resulting from damage to the skin barrier. Four weeks after discharge from the hospital, we observed gradual healing of the epidermis with slight scars. Anti-tuberculosis therapy was continued for 4 months after diagnosis of TEN without any adverse events. The timeline of the treatment of the patient was presented in  Figure 3 .

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old man presented with high fever (>40 °C), severe generalized pruritus, oral mucositis, and progressive skin sloughing covering >50% of his body ten days after postoperative adjuvant chemoimmunotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 59-year-old man with centrally located squamous cell lung carcinoma (T3N0M0) and active pulmonary tuberculosis received 4-drug ATT (HRZE) and 3 cycles of neoadjuvant sintilimab plus chemotherapy, followed by VATS left lower lobectomy. Adjuvant sintilimab and chemotherapy were continued postoperatively. Ten days later, he developed high fever (>40 °C), pruritus, massive trunk rashes, oral mucositis, and extensive epidermal necrolysis involving 95% of total body surface area.
subjective.past_medical_history: Squamous cell lung cancer (T3N0M0, invading left pulmonary artery, status-post VATS lobectomy); pulmonary tuberculosis on HRZE. No prior drug allergies or cutaneous adverse events during neoadjuvant phase.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports high fever, generalized pruritus, massive rash, skin sloughing, oral mucositis; denies respiratory, cardiac, or gastrointestinal complaints. Home medications: isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, sintilimab, chemotherapy. Allergies not documented prior to reaction.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (>40 °C). Massive maculopapular eruption on chest and abdomen; epidermal necrolysis and flaccid detachment involving approximately 95% of total body surface area. Oral mucositis present. Positive Nikolsky sign.
objective.routine_investigations: NLR: 3.48; PLR: 217.39; CRP: 53.28 mg/L; WBC: decreased secondary to chemotherapy; Chest CT (initial): tumor mass between left upper and lower lobes invading left pulmonary artery, concurrent pulmonary tuberculosis lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: VATS left lower lobectomy post-surgical pathology confirmed partial tumor response. Skin biopsy omitted due to financial constraints.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Sintilimab-induced severe Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) involving 95% total body surface area, in a patient with resected squamous cell lung carcinoma and concurrent pulmonary tuberculosis.
Confirmation: Clinical diagnosis of TEN based on sintilimab exposure, widespread epidermal detachment (>50%, total 95% BSA), oral mucositis, positive Nikolsky sign, and elevated inflammatory ratios (NLR 3.48, PLR 217.39, CRP 53.28 mg/L). Pulmonary tuberculosis was diagnosed by prior etiological and pathological confirmation, successfully treated with HRZE.
Differentials ruled out: Exfoliative dermatitis (ruled out by positive Nikolsky sign and >50% epidermal necrosis), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (<10% detachment vs 95% BSA), staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
Treatment & Outcome: Sintilimab discontinued immediately. Intravenous methylprednisolone 40 mg/day, transitioned to oral prednisone 60 mg/day; supportive wound care, nutritional support, analgesia, and levofloxacin 500 mg/day for skin barrier infection prophylaxis. Anti-tuberculosis therapy (HRZE) was maintained throughout. Epidermal healing with minor scars was observed at 4 weeks post-discharge, and ATT was successfully completed for 4 months post-TEN diagnosis without adverse events.
